newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish rightists cautious over joint campaign idea.
newsitem.headline: Polish rightists cautious over joint campaign idea.

text.p: The chiefs of Poland's two big rightist groupings, Solidarity Election Action (AWS) and ROP, were unenthusiastic on Monday about suggestions they field a joint list of candidates for this year's general elections.

The suggestion was made at the weekend by Jaroslaw Kaczynski, head of a party in the Solidarity trade union-led AWS alliance, who said that by joining forces the AWS and the Movement for the Reconstruction of Poland (ROP) could together gain 40 percent of the votes in the polls due around September. @

But ROP leader Jan Olszewski said on Monday that a common campaign for the lower house of parliament would probably benefit neither group, although they intended to field a joint list for the smaller, less powerful upper house, the Senate.
"Everything is possible and we have several months to the elections, but I don't think at the moment this is a good idea," Olszewski, a former prime minister, told private Radio Zet.
"We will march separately, but strike together," he said, repeating that the two groups intended to work together once they got into parliament -- hopefully with a clear majority. @
AWS spokesman Tomasz Tywonek told Reuters that the common list proposal was based on electoral studies he had not seen.
"This is a very important matter and would require a lot of thought," Tywonek said.
Rightist parties descended from the Solidarity movement, which toppled communism in 1989, fared disastrously in 1993 polls largely because they were hopelessly fragmented.
A coalition of ex-communists and a Peasant party rooted in the pre-1989 communist system have been in power since then. @
Last year Olszewski founded ROP while the Solidarity trade union grouped dozens of rightist parties into an alliance in which it retains clear dominance in order to preserve unity.
Recent opinion polls show AWS rivalling the ex-communists for the lead with both enjoying support of well over 20 percent. Support for the ROP is swinging above and well below 10 percent.

Although both share similar patriotic, pro-Catholic values and economic plans such as a sweeping mass privatisation of state assets, ROP refused to join the AWS for fear of being seen as just another party hanging on the union's coat-tails. @

Kaczynski said that by joining together, AWS and ROP could both free themselves from pressure from their extreme fringes who at the moment could blackmail their parties by threatening to defect to the other.

"Poland will not be served by the entry into parliament of opponents of NATO, Russophiles, or people sick with anti-Semitic obsession," Gazeta Wyborcza daily quoted Kaczynski as saying at a meeting of his Centre Alliance (PC) party.
The AWS now links some parties with views like those of the liberal, pro-market centrist opposition Union for Freedom (UW), with others who proclaim populist or syndicalist principles.
ROP's membership is less varied and more radical. @

A test of strength before the election could come with a referendum on May 25 when the country decides whether to accept a new draft Polish constitution agreed by the main government and opposition parties in parliament, but rejected by ROP and by the AWS which had drafted its own proposal.

Solidarity union chief Marian Krzaklewski called over the weekend for AWS supporters to vote against the parliamentary draft, but he had earlier been careful to say he did not view the referendum as predicting the outcome of the election.
